title: Which enumerable sets are computable?

based_on.title: Lecture notes in Computability Theory
based_on.pages: Version December 3, 2008; §40 Proposition 40.4, p.105, complement upper bound and marker sketch

based_on.title: 13. Cubbyhole Mathematics
based_on.pages: Proposition 4, marker sketch; fair discoveries and simultaneous-event decoder repaired

summary: Classify the indices of computable enumerable domains at the third existential level, using movable markers and an explicit halting decoder.
abstract: An enumeration can eventually confirm that a number belongs to a set, while deciding membership requires a terminating answer for every number. Given an index for an enumerable set, how hard is it to tell whether some decision procedure exists for that set? A second enumeration covering exactly the missing numbers gives a third-level upper bound in the arithmetical hierarchy. A matching lower bound comes from a construction with two possible outcomes: its output is cofinite when a specified condition holds, and otherwise the output can decide the halting problem. Ordered markers keep track of the numbers not yet enumerated. In the second case, access to the final output set certifies that a whole finite prefix of markers has settled, allowing a precise recovery of halting information. This proves the complete classification without promising a method for finding a decision procedure from an arbitrary positive index.
